doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Sessions and teaching in New Orleans
title: Second-tier R&B session work in New Orleans
summary: How the sessions worked: head arrangements, live takes, overtime tricks, baritone playing bass lines before electric bass, and union pay of forty to fifty dollars.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: To be a session musician?

To be a session musician yeah. I mean they would tire them out and all of them. So the second tier and all the people who probably wouldn’t be famous was trying to be famous, so they needed a band, so we would be on the second tier. So that was how I made some money in session work. And sometimes people come to me and say, “man I saw your name on a song in England” or something. I don’t know. They got the tapes from the — I don’t know who in the hell all those people are, I don’t have the slightest idea.
Right. It was just like, did you show up and play?
That’s right. That’s right. And we had the head. They didn’t have any arrangement. We’d put a head arrangement on it and we’d go and put something on it after they started singing.
Was most of that stuff done with everybody there, was it live?

Oh yeah, you had to do that. And then we had a trick, you make a mistake this time, you make a mistake the next time, and keep going round and round so you’d get overtime. Cause there wasn’t no sense in punching in, I mean everything had to go down, the vocalist, the band, the whole rhythm section so everybody had to do it. So we got our formulas for that too, so and all the sessions was union sessions and we had a formula for that also.
That’s funny. What would the typical horn section be, a couple of saxes and —

Oh baritone, [scats] playing the bass line with that, ‘cause that was before the electric basses came in you see. I saw the first electric bass I think Monk or one of the Montgomery brothers came through with Lionel Hampton and that’s the first electric bass I ever saw. But before, and I tell people before that anybody was a bass player because they’d get on a bass and just slap on, you couldn’t hear no changes like formal changes, you couldn’t hear nothing.
That’s right.
It could be anybody slapping on the bass man.
Right, they’re just picking up the percussive end of it.
Exactly.
I’ll be darned.
Man everybody played bass in them days. If they had a bass, come on man you can make the gig, you got a bass.
Oh get out.
I’m serious. But so that’s the way that was. So they needed a baritone especially [scats] all them low notes and all that kind of stuff. So baritone could always get a good gig on a session.
What would a session like that pay, do you remember?
Oh I guess about forty dollars. Union. It came through the union, maybe forty, fifty dollars. So it was all right.
And then how many tunes would you put down.

Many as you could get in three hour session. A session was three hours. And after three hours you went into overtime. So that’s where the money was time and a half or something, that’s when you were making a little money.
